newsitem.title: USA: U.S.-funded radio to broadcast to Burma, Vietnam.
newsitem.headline: U.S.-funded radio to broadcast to Burma, Vietnam.

text.p: A U.S.-funded radio station will begin beaming short-wave broadcasts to Burma and Vietnam next month despite complaints from Asia that the news services represent propaganda and violate other nations' independence.

Radio Free Asia, created by Congress as an Asian counterpart to the anti-communist Radio Free Europe and set up as a private corporation, said it would start service to Burma on Feb. 4 and Vietnam on Feb. 6.
Established in the spring of 1996 and working on a lean budget of $10 million a year, RFA began broadcasts in Mandarin Chinese on Sept. 29 and added Tibetan in early December.
Both services drew outrage from Beijing, which blasted RFA as "Cold War propaganda," accusing it of distorting the truth and freely interfering in the internal affairs of sovereign nations.

Last month, Hanoi also lashed out at plans to extend the broadcasts to Vietnam, accusing the United States of seeking to undermine stability in Asia and warning of the impact on renewed relations between the former foes.
Hanoi and Washington normalised diplomatic ties in 1995, two decades after the Vietnam war ended with the collapse of U.S-backed South Vietnam to the forces of the communist north.
Relations have progressed slowly since then, and the two countries have yet to achieve full economic and trade normalisation.

The U.S. broadcasts to Burma are certain to annoy that country's military rulers. Washington has criticised the State Law and Order Council (SLORC) for repressing anti-government student unrest and for its treatment of opposition leader Aung San Suu Kyi.
The United States also led United Nations' condemnation of the SLORC which resulted in a resolution by the world assembly rebuking Burma for suppressing opposition.
RFA said its Burmese service would begin with a half-hour morning programme, broadcast twice and repeated in the evening.

"News and commentaries will focus on Burma and regional developments related to that country," RFA said in a written statement. "Besides political, economic and social news, the programme will also carry features and commentaries on human rights, women's issues and the environment."

RFA noted that the Vietnamese service would begin on the eve of Tet, the Lunar New Year in Vietnam, and said its initial programme would broadcast news and commentary, music and entertainment related to this national holiday. Programmes would start at 30 minutes and expand eventually to one hour.
The radio station plans to extend broadcasts to Cambodia, Laos, and North Korea later this year.
"RFA will follow the strictest standards of objectivity, fairness and quality, avoiding polemics, propaganda, patisanship, and attacks on any person, government or nation," the statement said.
